newsitem.title: FINLAND: S&P SAYS SEES NINE COUNTRIES JOINING EMU IN 1999.
newsitem.headline: S&P SAYS SEES NINE COUNTRIES JOINING EMU IN 1999.

text.p: Credit rating institute Standard & Poor's expects nine of the European Union's 15 member states to enter the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union from the start in January 1999.

"Standard & Poor's believes that nine of ther 15 EU member states -- Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands -- likely will be judged eligible for EMU membership in 1998, when the final decision must be made," S&P said in its CreditWeek publication received on Tuesday.
It warned that Finland might want to opt out of EMU later.

France and Germany were "EMU's most creditworthy, as well as most politically important, supporters," S&P said, adding the two had to join regardless of the shape of their public finances for the single currency to be able to start on schedule.
"Austria, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands are also strong candidates, as they are likely to perform as well, or better, next year in budget-deficit terms," it said.

The credit ratings of the nine potential EMU candidates "should range within the 'AAA' and 'AA' rating categories within the monetary union," S&P said, noting this differed little from the countries' current sovereign ratings.
The dominant criterion for S&P's credit ratings of sovereigns participating in EMU will be their public finances, it said.
S&P will also factor in a so called "EMU secession risk".

"Despite economic convergence among the leading EMU candidates, some of the smaller member states may still face significant adjustment costs. Finland and Ireland, with economic structures markedly different from those of some of the larger EU states, are two possible examples," it said.
Faced with an economic shock, public opinion may come to question the lack of an exchange rate adjustment option.
"There is no legal provision in Maastricht for opting out of EMU in a crisis, but that possibility cannot be excluded," S&P said.
It added it believed that such a risk was "relatively small" for the nine strongest candidates.
S&P said the credit ratings of states remaining outside EMU would not be affected negatively on grounds of that alone.
"The credit ratings of EU sovereigns outside EMU .. should be unaffected, at least initially," it said.
